analysis.title: Global Markets Comment: The Fed as a Driver of Long-Term Rates
key_insights: GS argues that major shifts in long-term rate pricing have coincided with Fed policy shifts that made the prevailing distribution of the future funds rate look untenable, not with deeper structural drivers of neutral rates or major macro events.
The latest break higher in forward rates came alongside the Fed's shift to a new hiking cycle, not in response to news about the investment cycle, the fiscal position or the initial energy shock.
Earlier in October, longer-dated nominal and real yields reached levels not seen in over 20 years, then reversed somewhat.

Past episodes support the framework. In August 2011 calendar-based forward guidance at the zero lower bound lowered long-term rate expectations. In late 2018 and early 2019 the 2.5% peak of the hiking cycle, confirmed by cuts in July 2019, made it harder to price long-term rates above that level. From May 2022 the faster hikes to the highest funds rate since 2001 pushed the forward distribution up substantially.
Large macro events such as the GFC in 2008-2009 and COVID in 2020 did not coincide with the largest shifts in long-term rate expectations, even though the policy rate moved sharply in both.
The market appears to hold an assumed range for the funds rate based on realized history, Fed communication and the cyclical state. It adjusts only when a Fed policy shift challenges that range.

Since the 2022-2023 tightening, forward real rates drifted higher in two steps. The first began in late 2024 and was cemented around the April 2025 tariffs, taking forwards above the 2023 highs. The second was a sustained rise into new territory in July 2026.

The Iran war and energy price spike from late February 2026 marked the low in yields. The upward revision to AI capex expectations in June also showed economic resilience. But forward real rates moved above their prior range only in July, after the Fed signaled and then delivered hikes (July dissents in favor of hikes, Jackson Hole, September FOMC).
Because the funds rate troughed above 3.6% before rising again, investors may have lost faith in the 3-3.5% neutral rate range the Fed and others assumed.

Historically, deep forward rates have settled near the upper end of the prior funds rate range and have tracked the 16-quarter rolling maximum funds rate. Longer-dated OIS forwards peaked near 5.2% in October, close to the 5.33% effective funds rate peak of 2023-24 and well above the market-implied peak for this cycle.

Pushing forwards meaningfully above the prior cycle peak would imply an unusually high premium unless the market expects the Fed to hike above those levels. Markets have already struggled to hold forward pricing near that zone.

Relief would most likely come once the market is confident the hiking cycle has peaked and the next move is lower. If the funds rate peaks at 4-4.25% (GS modal forecast) or a hike or two beyond, deep forwards above 5% would look less plausible. History suggests the market may need to see the tightening cycle definitively end before reassessing.

GS says the Fed-centered narrative and the deficit-plus-AI-investment explanation for higher real rates are not in conflict. Policy shifts reflect an economy shaped by structural forces such as unwithdrawn fiscal support and rising AI investment demand, which have required a persistently higher rate structure.

risk_factors: If the Fed is willing to take rates beyond the prior cycle peak, forward rates would look less extended, so a more hawkish policy path is the upside risk to long-term yields.
The market may need to see the tightening cycle definitively end before it reassesses deep forward rates, so relief could come late.
Structural forces (unwithdrawn fiscal support, rising AI investment demand) keep the economy needing a higher rate structure.
GS cautions that the framework should not be taken too literally and that the timing implied in its illustration is not precise.

Exhibit 5 applies the GS Fed funds forecast to the same framework and suggests forward rates could anchor lower if the market acknowledges the funds rate has peaked.

tension_points.theme: deficit and AI funding vs Fed policy
tension_points.bull_case: The Fed-policy narrative says forward rates are anchored by the funds rate peak. If the market sees the tightening cycle ending around GS's 4-4.25% forecast, deep forwards above 5% would look less plausible and could ease.
tension_points.bear_case: The deficit-plus-AI-investment explanation says structural forces keep real rates high. GS says fiscal support not being withdrawn and rising AI investment demand are likely reasons the economy has needed a persistently higher rate structure.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Expectations of the policy cycle shifting further in a hawkish direction, with the market seeing the Fed willing to take rates beyond the prior cycle peak, would make forward rates above 5% look less extended.

theme_stances.key_argument: Shifts in long-term rate pricing track Fed policy shifts that challenge the market's assumed funds rate distribution, not structural or macro shocks.
theme_stances.evidence: largely through shifts in actual Fed policy ranges that the market learns

theme_stances.theme: forward rates anchored by funds rate peak
theme_stances.key_argument: Pushing deep forward rates well above the prior funds rate peak would imply an unusually high premium unless the Fed is expected to hike further.
theme_stances.evidence: more challenging to price meaningfully higher forward OIS rates
